subject: chem
title: Nitrogen Compounds
subtitle: Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins.
concept: Amines are derivatives of ammonia where H atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups; they act as bases and nucleophiles.
Amino acids contain both –NH₂ and –COOH groups; they form zwitterions at the isoelectric point.
Proteins are polyamides formed by peptide bonds between amino acids; primary structure determines all higher order structure.

notes.heading: Amines
items: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia. Primary amines (R–NH₂) have one alkyl/aryl group on nitrogen; secondary (R₂NH) have two; tertiary (R₃N) have three.

Basicity: the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton. Alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia — the alkyl group donates electron density to N (inductive effect), making the lone pair more available. Phenylamines (arylamines) are much weaker bases — the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation.
Preparation: reduce a nitrile with LiAlH₄ (R–CN + 4[H] → R–CH₂–NH₂); or reduce nitrobenzene with Sn/HCl to give phenylamine; or nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with excess NH₃.

notes.heading: Amino Acids and Proteins
items: Amino acids contain both –NH₂ and –COOH groups. They are amphoteric — acting as an acid (donating H⁺ from –COOH) or a base (accepting H⁺ on –NH₂). At the isoelectric point (pI), the amino acid exists as a zwitterion (–NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ simultaneously; net charge = 0).

Peptide bonds form by condensation between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another, releasing water. Hydrolysis (reflux with HCl(aq) or NaOH(aq)) breaks the peptide bonds back to individual amino acids.
Paper/TLC chromatography identifies amino acids after hydrolysis — Rf = distance spot moved / distance solvent moved. Spots are visualised with ninhydrin spray (purple colour).

definitions.body: A molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge simultaneously (at the isoelectric point); the net overall charge is zero.
The pH at which an amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion with zero net charge.
The –CO–NH– bond formed by condensation reaction between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another.

workedExamples.q: Explain why methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.

steps.text: Methylamine: CH₃NH₂. The CH₃ group donates electrons to N (inductive effect), increasing electron density on N.
Greater electron density on N → lone pair more available → more readily donates to H⁺.
Methylamine has a higher Kb (lower pKb) than NH₃ → stronger base.

mistakes: Confusing primary, secondary, tertiary amines with primary/secondary/tertiary alcohols — amines are classified by groups on N, not on C.
Stating phenylamine is a stronger base than ethylamine — it is weaker (lone pair delocalised into ring).
Forgetting that the zwitterion has NO net charge, despite having charged groups.
tips: Amine basicity order: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃ > arylamine (in gas phase; in water, solvation effects mean 2° often strongest).
Zwitterion at pI: draw with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻.
Paper chromatography of amino acids: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent.

flashcards.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ethylamine?
flashcards.a: The lone pair on N in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available to accept a proton.
An amino acid with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ groups; overall net charge = 0 at the isoelectric point.

flashcards.q: How is a peptide bond formed?
flashcards.a: Condensation reaction between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of another, releasing water → –CO–NH–.

flashcards.q: How are amines prepared from nitriles?
flashcards.a: Reduction with LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni catalyst): R–CN + 4[H] → R–CH₂–NH₂ (primary amine).
The pH at which an amino acid exists as a zwitterion with zero net charge.

flashcards.q: How are amino acids identified after protein hydrolysis?
flashcards.a: Paper/TLC chromatography followed by ninhydrin spray → purple spots; Rf values identify each amino acid.

questions.q: Which is the strongest base?
questions.exp: Ethylamine (primary alkylamine): alkyl group increases electron density on N → stronger base than NH₃. Phenylamine is weakest (lone pair delocalised into ring).

questions.q: At the isoelectric point, an amino acid exists as:
questions.exp: At pI, –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ are present simultaneously — the molecule is a zwitterion with zero net charge.

questions.q: What bond links amino acids in a protein?
questions.exp: The peptide bond (–CO–NH–) is formed by condensation between –COOH and –NH₂ groups of adjacent amino acids.

questions.q: Which reagent identifies amino acids on a chromatogram?
questions.exp: Ninhydrin spray produces purple spots where amino acids are present on paper/TLC chromatograms.

questions.q: How does LiAlH₄ convert a nitrile to an amine?
questions.exp: LiAlH₄ provides H⁻ (hydride ions) to reduce the –CN group to –CH₂NH₂ — a four-hydrogen reduction.

questions.q: What reagent converts a primary amine into an amide?
questions.exp: RCOCl + R'NH₂ → RCONHR' + HCl. Acyl chlorides react vigorously with primary amines to give secondary amides. The reaction proceeds without a catalyst because the acyl chloride is much more reactive than a carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Why are aliphatic amines (e.g. methylamine) stronger bases than ammonia?
opts: Alkyl groups are electron-withdrawing, increasing the positive charge on N
Alkyl groups are electron-donating, increasing electron density on N
Alkyl groups decrease the size of the lone pair
Methylamine has a lower pKa than ammonia
questions.exp: Alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen by the inductive effect, making the lone pair more available for protonation. More available lone pair = stronger base. CH₃NH₂ has pKb ~3.4 vs NH₃ pKb ~4.7.

questions.q: How is phenylamine (aniline) synthesised from nitrobenzene?
opts: Reduction with Sn/HCl under reflux, then NaOH
questions.exp: C₆H₅NO₂ + 3[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + H₂O. Tin (Sn) and concentrated HCl reduce the nitro group. The initial product is the phenylammonium salt; NaOH is then added to liberate free phenylamine.

questions.q: At the isoelectric point of an amino acid, the species present is:
questions.exp: At the isoelectric point (pI), the amino acid exists predominantly as the zwitterion with both charges present but net charge zero. The –COOH donates its proton to –NH₂, giving –COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺ simultaneously.

questions.q: What colour does ninhydrin spray give with amino acids on a TLC plate?
questions.exp: Ninhydrin reacts with the α-amino group of amino acids to produce a purple/violet compound (Ruhemann's purple). This is used to visualise amino acid spots on TLC or paper chromatography plates.

questions.q: Which of these amines is the weakest base?
questions.exp: Phenylamine is the weakest base because the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring's π system, making it far less available for protonation. Pkb of phenylamine ~9.4 vs NH₃ ~4.7.

questions.q: What is the product when a nitrile is reduced with LiAlH₄?
questions.exp: R–CN + 4[H] → R–CH₂–NH₂. LiAlH₄ reduces the C≡N triple bond fully to give a primary amine with one more carbon than the nitrile. This is a useful chain-lengthening route in synthesis.

questions.q: Which reaction produces an amide bond (peptide bond)?
opts: Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of another
questions.exp: The peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms by condensation between the carboxyl group (–COOH) of one amino acid and the amino group (–NH₂) of another, releasing water. This linkage forms the primary structure of proteins.

questions.q: A primary amine is treated with HCl. What type of product forms?
questions.exp: R–NH₂ + HCl → R–NH₃⁺Cl⁻. Amines act as Brønsted bases, accepting H⁺ from HCl to form an alkylammonium salt. These salts are typically white solids, soluble in water.

questions.q: Why is paper/TLC chromatography used to identify amino acids after protein hydrolysis?
opts: Amino acids are coloured so they can be seen directly
Each amino acid has a characteristic Rf value; spots are visualised with ninhydrin
Amino acids form precipitates at the solvent front
The technique separates amino acids by molecular mass
questions.exp: After acid hydrolysis, the mixture of amino acids is spotted on TLC and developed. Each amino acid travels a characteristic distance (Rf). Ninhydrin spray reveals the spots as purple marks. Rf values identify each amino acid by comparison with standards.

questions.q: How is phenylamine (aniline) prepared from nitrobenzene?
questions.exp: Nitrobenzene + Sn + conc. HCl → phenylammonium salt → phenylamine on addition of NaOH. Sn/HCl reduces the nitro group.

questions.q: Phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia because:
opts: The lone pair on N is donated into the benzene ring (delocalised)
The N–H bond is too strong
questions.exp: The lone pair on N is partially delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring, making it less available to accept a proton.

questions.q: What type of reaction forms a peptide bond between two amino acids?
questions.exp: A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms by condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of another, releasing H₂O.

questions.q: At the isoelectric point of an amino acid, the species present is:
questions.exp: At the isoelectric point (pI), the amino acid exists as a zwitterion — net charge is zero but it carries both +1 and −1 groups.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a halogenoalkane to a primary amine?
opts: Excess concentrated NH₃ in a sealed tube
questions.exp: RX + excess NH₃ (ethanol, sealed tube, heat) → RNH₂ + HX. Excess NH₃ prevents further alkylation to secondary/tertiary amines.

questions.q: Ethylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid. The product is:
questions.exp: Amines are bases: C₂H₅NH₂ + HCl → C₂H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (ethylammonium chloride). This is an acid-base neutralisation.

questions.q: A primary amine reacts with an acyl chloride to give:
questions.exp: RCONH–R′ (secondary amide) forms: RCOCl + R′NH₂ → RCONHR′ + HCl. The –CONH– linkage is a secondary amide.

questions.q: Which of these is an amino acid?
questions.exp: Glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) has both an –NH₂ group and a –COOH group on the same carbon — the definition of an α-amino acid.

questions.q: Ninhydrin is used to detect amino acids on a TLC plate. What colour does it produce?
questions.exp: Ninhydrin reacts with α-amino acids (and amines) to produce a characteristic purple/violet colour (Ruhemann's purple).

questions.q: In paper chromatography of amino acids, Rf = 0.6 means:
opts: The spot moved 60% as far as the solvent front
60% of the amino acid was retained
The spot is 60 mm from origin
questions.exp: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front = 0.6 means the spot travelled 60% of the total solvent distance.
